summary: Children extend telling time to reading analogue clocks to the nearest five minutes, writing that time in 12-hour digital notation (h:mm with a colon), labelling it a.m. or p.m., and rewriting it in 24-hour notation (hh:mm). The core procedure: count the clock's 12 intervals in fives so each numeral maps to its minute value (numeral 4 -> 20 minutes, not 4); use a vertical 12-to-6 partition to decide 'past' (right) versus 'to' (left) the hour, with 'to' times named against the NEXT hour; anchor a.m./p.m. to real daily events, understanding that each clock time occurs twice a day, split at noon and midnight; and convert to 24-hour time (from 1 p.m. onwards add 12 to the hour, so 3:40 p.m. = 15:40; a.m. hours stay the same, written with two digits, e.g. 8:05 a.m. = 08:05; the 12 o'clock hour after midnight becomes 00, e.g. 12:15 a.m. = 00:15, and the noon hour stays 12, e.g. 12:15 p.m. = 12:15). Activities below include a manipulable clock (preferred), practice/discrimination tasks, a static labelling scaffold, and an elicitation conversation, each with its own pedagogical purpose.
misconceptions: Reads the numeral the minute hand points to as the minutes (points to 4 -> '4 minutes past')
Confuses times past and times to the hour
Insecure 5 times-table blocks fluent counting of minutes
Writes a decimal point instead of a colon (3.25)
Thinks there are 100 minutes in an hour, so 50 past 3 = 50 to 4
Confuses a.m. and p.m. (1 a.m. 'should be' 1 p.m. because it feels late); doesn't know noon/midnight or that each time occurs twice a day

activities.title: Drag the minute hand and watch the count-in-fives and digital readout
steps: Drag the minute hand around a moveable-hands clock and watch a 'count in 5s' tape (5, 10, 15, 20...) unroll around the rim as a digital readout ticks alongside.
Pause when the minute hand reaches the numeral 4 and confirm the tape and readout say 20 minutes, not 4 — then do the same for numeral 8 (40 minutes).
Watch a vertical 12-to-6 line shade one colour on the right (past) and another on the left (to), and read 3:40 aloud as 'twenty TO four'.

Flip an a.m./p.m. toggle that slides a marker along a day-strip so the SAME hand position recurs 12 hours later — once in the morning (e.g. 8 o'clock breakfast, a.m.) and again 12 hours on in the evening (p.m.).
Write the shown time as h:mm using a colon with its a.m./p.m. label (e.g. 3:25 p.m.), then rewrite it in 24-hour notation (e.g. 15:25; 8:05 a.m. = 08:05).
activities.insight: Each clock numeral stands for its five-times value, 'to' times are named against the next hour, and every clock position recurs 12 hours later, so each clock time happens twice in one day, split at noon and midnight.

activities.title: Read, convert and sort: discrimination practice
steps: Match analogue clock faces (with a.m./p.m. given) to their 12-hour and 24-hour digital times (and back), e.g. twenty to four in the afternoon = 3:40 p.m. = 15:40.
Answer discriminating questions such as 'Is 3:40 forty past three or twenty to four?'
Sort daily activities (breakfast, school, bedtime) into a.m. and p.m.
Write a shown clock as h:mm, using a colon.
activities.insight: Secure practice separates past from to, maps analogue to digital, and connects a.m./p.m. to everyday events, while surfacing residual errors.

activities.title: Label the fives on a fixed clock face (scaffold)
steps: On a static clock, tap each numeral to reveal its minute value (1 -> 5, 2 -> 10, ... 8 -> 40, ... 11 -> 55).
Read the revealed values aloud in order round the rim to rehearse the five-times link.
Point to the 12-6 line and say which numerals sit on the 'past' side (1–5) and which on the 'to' side (7–11), noting that 12 (o'clock) and 6 (half past) sit on the line itself.
activities.insight: Each numeral labels a five-minute step, and the rim splits into a past side and a to side.

activities.title: Talk about your day: eliciting a.m./p.m.
steps: Answer questions like 'What time do you have breakfast? Is that a.m. or p.m.?' and 'What about when you go to bed?'
Place named daily events on a day-timeline split at noon and midnight.
Identify which 12 o'clock is noon and which is midnight, and say where on the timeline a.m. changes to p.m. and back.
Explain, for a given event, whether the clock time is in the morning or after noon.
Given a digital time with no label (e.g. 3:40), say how many different moments in one day it could be and why.
activities.insight: a.m./p.m. labels connect to real daily events and to the noon/midnight split, so the same clock time can occur twice a day — once before noon and once after.

checkQuestion: Set reading and writing tasks and WATCH how the child works, never asking them to define terms: (1) Hand the child a moveable-hands analogue clock set to 3:40, then to 4:25: 'Read each one to me and write it as it would look on a digital clock.' (2) Show a 12-hour digital display 3:40: 'Say this time in words — is it past or to the hour?' (3) 'It's 8 o'clock and I'm eating breakfast — is that a.m. or p.m.? Now it's 8 o'clock and I'm going to bed — a.m. or p.m.?' Watch whether they count round in fives and land on past/to correctly, write with a colon, and separate a.m. from p.m.
checkAnswer: Counts the intervals in fives (numeral 8 -> 40) rather than reading the numeral as minutes; reads 3:40 as 'twenty to four'; writes '4:25' with a colon; states breakfast 8 o'clock = a.m. and bedtime 8 o'clock = p.m., showing each time occurs twice a day.
